title: MappingPerimenopause: A Spotlight on Women’s Brain Health: Mapping In Vivo Brain Dynamics across the Perimenopausal Years.
summary:
The menopause transition is a significant phase in the lives of most women, accompanied by substantial physical and psychological changes. The perimenopause in particular – the transitional period preceding the final menstrual period – is of considerable clinical relevance: up to 80% of women report burdensome symptoms such as hot flushes, night sweats, sleep disturbances, mood changes, and memory problems. These complaints are not only immediately distressing, but are increasingly recognised as potential risk factors for later neurodegenerative disease. Despite this clinical importance, female brain health during this life phase remains poorly understood – existing evidence is largely based on animal studies or cross-sectional data that do not adequately capture the dynamic nature of the perimenopausal transition.

MappingPerimenopause therefore investigates, over a period of three years, how the perimenopause affects the brain and mental health of 300 late-perimenopausal women aged 40 to 55 years at study entry. At three time points (baseline, 1.5 years, and 3 years), brain scans, neurocognitive tests, and stool and hair samples are collected. In addition, blood samples and clinical and psychosocial data are gathered every 6 months, while perimenopausal symptoms are continuously tracked using the Clue app (BioWink).

To strengthen the reliability and broader applicability of the findings, the study data will be compared and analysed together with health data from large population-based studies – such as the UK Biobank, which holds data from hundreds of thousands of people. MappingPerimenopause is also part of an international research network in which scientists worldwide pool and jointly analyse brain data (the ENIGMA consortium). The principal investigator leads the working group on hormones, brain health, and menopause within this network.

The overarching aim is to identify risk and resilience factors as a basis for targeted prevention and intervention strategies to promote the brain and mental health of women during and after this transitional phase.
conditions: The study investigates perimenopausal symptoms (ICD-10: N95.1) in women aged 40 to 55 years in late perimenopause (amenorrhea ≥ 60 days, according to STRAW criteria). Climacteric symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and sleep disturbances are assessed using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS). Women in postmenopause as well as those with surgically or medically induced menopause are excluded at study baseline.

interventions.name:
This monocentric, prospective observational study investigates the effects of the perimenopause on brain and mental health using an integrated biopsychosocial approach over a period of three years. A total of 300 late-perimenopausal women aged 40 to 55 years at baseline will be enrolled.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Late perimenopausal (i.e. amenorrhoea of at least 60 days according to STRAW criteria)
- Perimenopausal symptoms (e.g. hot flushes, night sweats, sleep disturbances, etc., assessed by standardised questionnaire, MRS)
- Written informed consent to participate in the study
- Existing health insurance
Exclusion criteria:
- Use of hormonal contraceptives
- Use of hormone replacement therapy at study entry (initiation during the study is not an exclusion or discontinuation criterion)
- Pregnancy
- Hysterectomy and/or bilateral oophorectomy, or other surgical interventions leading to permanent cessation of menstruation
- Conditions associated with irregular menstrual cycles, such as polycystic ovary syndrome
- Physical illnesses that, by nature or severity, may interfere with the planned assessments or influence the parameters under investigation (e.g. focal neurological disorders, cancer, cardiac or pulmonary disease, renal disease, chronic pain conditions)
- Currently manifest psychiatric disorders (e.g. substance dependence (excluding nicotine), schizophrenia, bipolar disorder)
- Psychotropic medication
- Substance misuse or illicit drug use
- History of moderate or severe head trauma requiring hospitalisation
- Neurological conditions (e.g. brain tumour, stroke) that may affect brain structure or function
- MRI contraindications (e.g. metal implants or devices such as cardiac pacemakers, claustrophobia, sensorineural hearing loss of 30 dB or above, tinnitus)
